source_anchor: Spinoza Ethics Part I prop.14 + def.6; Part III preface; Part V prop.42; SEP "Spinoza" §3
instance: Spinoza's monism (substance monism) and parallelism (one substance under attributes of thought and extension) deny mind-body causal interaction in the Cartesian sense. State the structural reason why parallelism follows from monism, and identify one consequence for the question of free will.

answer_features.claim: substance monism: only one substance (Deus sive Natura), modes are modifications of it
parallelism: thought and extension are attributes of the same substance, ordered identically
alt_phrasings: order of ideas equals order of things
thought and extension are two attributes
mind and body express same modification

answer_features.claim: consequence: free will as causal autonomy is illusory; freedom is adequate understanding
alt_phrasings: free will reduces to ignorance of causes

candidate_responses.text: Monism: one substance, Deus sive Natura, with infinite attributes; modes are its modifications. Parallelism: thought and extension are two of those attributes, expressing the same order of modifications. Consequence: free will as Cartesian causal autonomy collapses; what Spinoza calls freedom is adequate understanding of one's own determination.
One substance, two attributes ordered identically; therefore mind cannot causally push body. Freedom in Spinoza is reframed as understanding necessity, not exemption from it.
